chapterTitle: Chapter I • Welcome & The Workplace English Foundation (00:00 – 05:30)
speaker: Louie
text: Hello, hello there, everyone, and how are you today? Is it—is it Simone? Is that correct, or Simon?

speaker: Simone
text: Simone. I'm fine! I'm Fixed: “at the office” (note-taker wrote: “in office”) right now, at the end of my workday. But I'm doing well.

speaker: Louie
text: Very good, very good! Well, thank you very much for your time today. We chatted briefly before, but I would love to hear directly from you: what brings us here today?

speaker: Simone
text: My company requested us to take some courses to improve my English, and of course for all my colleagues. In the past, we had English courses with one teacher and typically four people from my company. I think it will be much more helpful to have a one-to-one lesson to get more speaking practice.

speaker: Louie
text: Practice makes a world of difference! And how much English do you speak in your company presently?

speaker: Simone
text: Often in writing emails. We have connections with our Fixed: “headquarters” (note-taker wrote: “headquarter”) where we have to explain issues or problems that our customers report to us. Typically we do that by email, but sometimes we have presentations or meetings with customers and headquarters, so we have to understand what our colleagues say and explain the customer's reasoning.

speaker: Louie
text: You know what, I have to commend you! Your English has a very interesting and strong foundation. You clearly have a good logical process of English.

speaker: Simone
text: Really? That's encouraging.

speaker: Louie
text: Listening to you talk even now in your response, I can see it in your explanation of communicating with different counterparts and different stakeholders. You are actually quite quick at answering! Where you can really get improvement is definitely with your rhythm and pronunciation.

speaker: Simone
text: Okay, that makes sense.

speaker: Louie
text: With my other students, that comes with light exercises and lots of conversation. You will naturally start to imitate natural cadence, and fluency becomes second nature. We'll look at two kinds of vocabulary: general vocabulary and workplace vocabulary.

speaker: Simone
text: Okay, perfect.

speaker: Louie
text: Before we go any further, what do you do in your daily role, if I may ask?

speaker: Simone
text: I work in technical support, so my job is to troubleshoot and resolve problems for our customers. We offer alternative solutions with our systems for their machines, and we collaborate with colleagues in sales to propose products that complete the customer's setup.

speaker: Louie
text: Fantastic answer! What you've done before has clearly worked. We call it a rebuttal—your ability to answer is great. You are very quick and you give precise answers. Really impressive!

chapterTitle: Chapter II • Workplace Vocabulary & The System Demo (05:34 – 15:00)
speaker: Louie
text: Let's talk about some vocabulary and keep it within your realm. Can you tell me what a trade-off is? How would you describe or define it?

speaker: Simone
text: Trade-off? It's a sort of balance between two or more things.

speaker: Louie
text: Exactly that! For example, the trade-off of buying an expensive phone is that it has higher quality, but it is much more costly. You balance one benefit against another.

speaker: Simone
text: Yes, exactly. A compromise.

speaker: Louie
text: Very good! And what about the word bottleneck in business or systems engineering?

speaker: Simone
text: I know what it means in my mind, but it's difficult to explain in English! It is a major difficulty or constraint for a specific scenario.

speaker: Louie
text: A bottleneck is when part of the process or operation cannot keep up with other parts of the business. For example, your sales team might be selling loads of services, but HR has a bottleneck because they cannot hire and train enough staff to keep up with customer demand. Do you ever get bottlenecks in your job?

speaker: Simone
text: We have cases of bottlenecks with our products. For example, when a customer uses our system in their machines, but the Fixed: “project or product” (note-taker wrote: “proca product”) we sold does not fit the specific requirements of the customer, it creates a delay for the whole project.

speaker: Louie
text: Very good real-world example! It creates a bottleneck within their process, and the rest of the company suffers. Next is the idiom in the loop. Have you heard that before?

speaker: Simone
text: Yes, we use it often in emails.

speaker: Louie
text: Before we unpack that, let me mention: I give comprehensive notes! About half an hour after class, you get an interactive companion document. Let me share my screen to show you the demo so this can take the pressure off taking notes while we chat.

speaker: Simone
text: Okay, great!

speaker: Louie
text: Here is the interactive transcript with exact timestamps. If you hover over any highlighted word, it tells you what it means, its CEFR level (B2–C2), and pronunciation. If you click on it, the details appear in the sticky side panel with British RP audio so you can listen anytime.

speaker: Simone
text: Quaint... serendipity. Very good, thank you!

speaker: Louie
text: And if you just want to recap the vocabulary without scrolling the transcript, you go to the dictionary tab with nice cards. I publish it on GitHub Pages with one single link forever, so you never have to search through files. The notes are already there for you!

speaker: Simone
text: That is very convenient and helpful. Thank you!

speaker: Louie
text: Now, let's return to in the loop and its opposite, out of the loop.

speaker: Simone
text: Yes, in the email context: if someone is added to an email conversation, they are in the loop. On the contrary, if you are not receiving communication, you are out of the loop.

speaker: Louie
text: Spot on! That's how we build business vocabulary. But I also believe in free-form conversation because we learn so much more natural language that way.

chapterTitle: Chapter III • Quick Word Association & The Italian Table (15:10 – 20:30)
speaker: Louie
text: Let's do a quick exercise where we describe words from categories without saying the actual word. I'll send you a link to pick a category and describe something for me to guess. Ready?

speaker: Simone
text: I chose food! Let's start.

speaker: Simone
text: It is a fruit that is on a particular plant, and you use it to Fixed: “make wine” (note-taker wrote: “do the wine”).

speaker: Louie
text: To make wine—grapes!

speaker: Simone
text: Correct! Next one: this is a typical first course Fixed: “first course (primo piatto)” (note-taker wrote: “first plate”) that we make with mushrooms.

speaker: Louie
text: Is it pizza or pasta?

speaker: Simone
text: No, it's risotto!

speaker: Louie
text: Oh, risotto! Fantastic. Earlier, you mentioned grapes grow on trees, but in English we say grapes grow on vines Fixed: “vines / vineyard” (note-taker wrote: “Vinegard”). Do you enjoy wine?

speaker: Simone
text: No, Fixed: “I don't drink wine” (note-taker wrote: “I don't drink the wines”) at all!

speaker: Louie
text: Fair enough! Now it's your turn to pick a category for me to describe.

speaker: Simone
text: Animals!

speaker: Louie
text: Okay, three, two, one: black and white, native to China, loves bamboo.

speaker: Simone
text: It's a panda!

speaker: Louie
text: Exactly right! Next: a small little bug, and it glows in the dark.

speaker: Simone
text: I know what it looks like, but I don't know the name in English!

speaker: Louie
text: It's a firefly! Next: the king of the jungle.

speaker: Simone
text: The lion!

speaker: Louie
text: And this bird flies incredibly fast and drinks nectar from blossoms.

speaker: Simone
text: I understand the animal, but I don't remember the name in English or Italian!

speaker: Louie
text: It's a hummingbird (colibrì in Italian)! Its wings flap so fast that it can hover completely still.

chapterTitle: Chapter IV • Life in Bologna, Twins & Family Ties (20:38 – 26:10)
speaker: Louie
text: Whereabouts in Italy are you located?

speaker: Simone
text: I'm in Bologna, in the north of Italy. Do you know it?

speaker: Louie
text: Yes! Although the place I normally visited was Lucca in Tuscany, where my former partner's family lived. But now I'm in Hanoi, Vietnam, studying Vietnamese at university for international business. Before moving here, I worked in historical restoration, rebuilding old buildings that are 600 to 700 years old.

speaker: Simone
text: Rebuilding historic buildings—that sounds like a very nice job!

speaker: Louie
text: What are your interests and passions? What do you like to do in your spare time?

speaker: Simone
text: I spend a lot of time with my work, and with my family because I have twin daughters who are four years old!

speaker: Louie
text: Congratulations! Wow, twins! At four years old, are you able to sleep through the night now?

speaker: Simone
text: Yes, they are very good—they sleep all night now, except when they are ill or something goes wrong.

speaker: Louie
text: And are twins common in your family?

speaker: Simone
text: Not so much. In our extended family we had some relatives Fixed: “relatives” (note-taker wrote: “parents”) who had twins, but they aren't very close to me.

speaker: Louie
text: We say relatives or extended family! How was the moment when you and your wife found out?

speaker: Simone
text: When the doctor said it to me and my wife, I turned totally red from shock! But now, it's very beautiful having twin daughters. They have a very special dynamic together.

speaker: Louie
text: They share a special bond with each other that lasts a lifetime. It's truly wonderful.

speaker: Simone
text: Yes! Especially when I try to teach something to one of them, the other sister who isn't involved immediately steps in to help her.

speaker: Louie
text: That is so sweet! Do you have siblings yourself? Brothers and sisters?

speaker: Simone
text: Yes, I have an older brother who is 48, and an older sister who is 44.

chapterTitle: Chapter V • Board Games, Gaming & A New Zealand Honeymoon (26:14 – 41:35)
speaker: Louie
text: Before family life kept you so busy, what were your hobbies and interests?

speaker: Simone
text: Especially with my wife, we like playing video games together. And we have a group of friends where we really enjoy playing Fixed: “board games” (note-taker wrote: “boarding games”).

speaker: Louie
text: What board games are you playing, and what video games do you and your wife play?

speaker: Simone
text: With my wife, I play a mobile game that is very competitive with 3v3 teams. And on PlayStation, we are playing God of War: Ragnarok. Before the twins, my friend and I completed Horizon Zero Dawn on Saturday afternoons.

speaker: Louie
text: Horizon Zero Dawn is brilliant, and I love the cinematic scale of God of War—it feels just like a movie. What about your board game collection?

speaker: Simone
text: Between my friend and me, we have a complete library of board games. It depends on how much time we have and how many people are playing.

speaker: Louie
text: For our next lesson, let's talk about board game mechanics! For homework, pick two board games from your shelf, and I'll pick two from mine to discuss. I go to a board game night once a week here in Hanoi.

speaker: Simone
text: In our group, we are six or seven people: Fixed: “three couples” (note-taker wrote: “three capital”) and two other friends. One couple is often abroad, but my wife, my best friend, his wife, and I meet whenever we can.

speaker: Louie
text: How long have you known your best friend?

speaker: Simone
text: Since birth! Our families were friends, so he was two when I was born. We have had a lifelong friendship.

speaker: Louie
text: What's your favorite board game to play with him?

speaker: Simone
text: Definitely 7 Wonders! It's a game where you build your civilization Fixed: “civilization” (note-taker wrote: “civil team”). To win, you collect victory points through card drafting.

speaker: Simone
text: You have military cards, science cards, and cards for city economy. You build card combos across three distinct eras Fixed: “eras / ages” (note-taker wrote: “three era”) to maximize your score.

speaker: Louie
text: That sounds reminiscent of Civilization! Every night, my international friends and I play one game of Risk online. It is fiercely competitive.

speaker: Louie
text: At our Hanoi board game meetup, we also play the social deduction game Werewolf or Mafia with up to 30 people.

speaker: Simone
text: In Italy, that game is called Fixed: “Lupus in Tabula” (note-taker wrote: “Lupo Lupis”)! It's very well known.

speaker: Louie
text: We play it in Vietnamese with custom rules and constant rule evolution. I always tell myself I'll keep quiet, but to no avail—I always talk too much!

chapterTitle: Chapter VI • Cultural Contrasts, Lord of the Rings & Looking Ahead (41:40 – 50:50)
speaker: Louie
text: In Vietnam, eating street food outside is completely normal—you'll see an entire family on one motorbike! Do you eat out often in Bologna?

speaker: Simone
text: In the morning, coffee and breakfast outside, but in the evening we almost always cook and eat at home.

speaker: Louie
text: Have you traveled much abroad? Have you ever visited England?

speaker: Simone
text: Not yet, but I would love to visit England with my family. My wife is a huge Harry Potter fan, so seeing the studio tour and film locations would be wonderful.

speaker: Simone
text: We don't have an HBO subscription yet, but she is very eager to watch the new television series when it arrives.

speaker: Louie
text: I read all the Harry Potter books to my younger brother. Harry Potter and the Fixed: “Prisoner of Azkaban” (note-taker wrote: “Prison of Azkaban”) had such a great movie adaptation.

speaker: Simone
text: My favorite cinematic work of all time is Fixed: “The Lord of the Rings” (note-taker wrote: “Lord of the Ring”). I read the entire trilogy before the third film came out.

speaker: Simone
text: When my wife and I got married, we spent our honeymoon road-tripping through New Zealand!

speaker: Louie
text: New Zealand for your honeymoon! What an extraordinary adventure. What was your itinerary?

speaker: Simone
text: We started in Auckland, rented a car, and drove down the North Island to Wellington. We visited Fixed: “Hobbiton” (note-taker wrote: “the Hobbiton Town”) in Matamata, and the rolling green scenery was breathtaking—just like the movie.

speaker: Simone
text: It felt so strange to be standing in a place you know is a fantasy realm from films, but you are physically right there.

speaker: Louie
text: The films are absolute cinematic masterpieces. But reading Tolkien can be so dense with songs and history—it takes real dedication!

speaker: Simone
text: Yes, especially the early chapter of The Fellowship of the Ring with Fixed: “Tom Bombadil” (note-taker wrote: “Tom Bombay”)—that part is notoriously slow to get through.

speaker: Louie
text: Simone, you have expressed so many fascinating thoughts today! Your vocabulary and foundation are far stronger than you give yourself credit for.

speaker: Simone
text: Thank you, Louie! Sometimes when I try to speak English, I feel tongue-tied and I freeze up because I search for a specific term and get locked in the sentence.

speaker: Louie
text: That happens to every language learner! In our lessons, you never have to worry about perfection. Chatting about board games and real experiences gives us plenty of food for thought. For next lesson, prepare two board games from your collection, and we will build our vocabulary together!

speaker: Simone
text: That sounds wonderful. Thank you very much, Louie!

speaker: Louie
text: You are very welcome, Simone. Have a lovely evening in Bologna, give my best to your family, and I'll see you next lesson!
